questions.prompt: A voltage step (0 V to \(V_{s}\) at \(t=0\)) is applied to an RC low-pass filter with the capacitor initially discharged. What is the output \(v_{o}(t)\) for t > 0?
questions.explanation:
The step response is \(V_{s}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) (reader Eq. 1.82): it starts at 0 and rises exponentially toward \(V_{s}\).
• \(V_{s}\ e^{-t/\tau}\) is a decay starting at \(V_{s}\) (the response of a charged capacitor discharging, or the impulse response shape).
• The exponent must be \(-t/\tau\) (dimensionless), not \(-t\tau\).
• A capacitor voltage cannot change instantly through a resistor, so the output smooths the step.

questions.prompt: After a step is applied to an RC low-pass filter, how long does the output take to reach about 63% of its final value?
questions.explanation: At \(t=\tau\): \(1-e^{-1}=0.632\), i.e., about 63% of the final value. After \(2\tau\) it is 86.5%, after \(5\tau\) it is 99.3% (essentially settled).

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter with \(\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}\) (capacitor initially discharged) receives a 5 V pulse of width 2 ms (5 V from \(t=0\) to 2 ms, then back to 0 V). What is the output at \(t=3\ \mathrm{ms}\)?
questions.explanation:
Phase 1 (0 < t < 2 ms): \(v_{o}=5(1-e^{-t/\tau})\). At \(t=2\ \mathrm{ms}\): \(v_{o}=5(1-e^{-2})=4.323\ \mathrm{V}\).
Phase 2 (t > 2 ms): the input is 0, so the capacitor discharges from 4.323 V: \(v_{o}=4.323\cdot e^{-(t-2\ \mathrm{ms})/\tau}\). At \(t=3\ \mathrm{ms}\): \(4.323\times e^{-1}=1.59\ \mathrm{V}\).
Check by superposition: a pulse is a step minus a delayed step: \(5(1-e^{-3})-5(1-e^{-1})=4.751-3.161=1.59\ \mathrm{V}\checkmark\).
Common mistake: restarting the clock and using \(4.323\ e^{-3}\), or continuing to charge toward 5 V.
questions.figure_alt: A 5 V, 2 ms input pulse (solid) and the RC output (dashed) rising then decaying.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has time constant \(\tau\) and starts discharged. A 2 V step is applied at \(t=t_{0}\) (not at \(t=0\)). What is \(v_{o}(t)\) for \(t>t_{0}\)?
questions.explanation:
Time invariance: delaying the input by \(t_{0}\) delays the output by \(t_{0}\), so t is replaced by \(t-t_{0}\) in the exponent. Linearity scales the unit-step response by 2.
• \(2(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) forgets the delay (the output would start rising before the step arrives).
• Dropping the factor of 2 is the response to a 1 V step.
• The exponent needs division by \(\tau\), not multiplication.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has \(\tau=0.5\ \mathrm{ms}\). After a step input from rest, how long does the output take to reach 90% of its final value?
questions.explanation:
\(1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.9\) ⇒ \(e^{-t/\tau}=0.1\) ⇒ \(t=\tau\ \ln 10=2.303\tau\).
\(t=2.303\times 0.5\ \mathrm{ms}=1.151\ \mathrm{ms}\).
Common mistake: answering \(t=\tau=0.5\ \mathrm{ms}\) (that is the 63% point).

questions.prompt: A 5 V pulse of width 10 µs drives an RC low-pass with \(\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}\) (capacitor initially discharged). Roughly what is the peak output voltage?
options: 5 V, because the input reaches 5 V
questions.explanation:
The pulse is much shorter than \(\tau\), so the capacitor barely charges. Exact: peak \(=5(1-e^{-0.01})=49.75\ \mathrm{mV}\), which is \(\approx 5\times(10\ \mu\mathrm{s}/1\ \mathrm{ms})=50\ \mathrm{mV}\) (using \(1-e^{-x}\approx x\) for small x).
The filter output looks like a scaled copy of the impulse response, with size set by the pulse AREA \((5\ \mathrm{V}\times 10\ \mu\mathrm{s})\) divided by \(\tau\).
• 5 V would need the pulse to last many time constants.
• 63% applies only after one full \(\tau\) of input.
• 0.5 V is 10 times too large (would be a 100 µs pulse).

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter's capacitor starts at 2 V when a step input of 5 V is applied \((\tau=RC)\). What is \(v_{o}(t)\) for \(t\ge 0\)?
questions.explanation:
General first-order response: \(v(t)=v_{\mathrm{final}}+(v_{\mathrm{initial}}-v_{\mathrm{final}})e^{-t/\tau}=5+(2-5)e^{-t/\tau}=5-3e^{-t/\tau}\). It starts at 2 V and approaches 5 V.
• \(5(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) starts at 0 V (assumes the capacitor was discharged).
• \(5-2e^{-t/\tau}\) uses the initial voltage rather than the initial DISTANCE to the final value (starts at 3 V).
• \(2+5(1-e^{-t/\tau})\) heads to 7 V: the step contributes only the 3 V difference, not the full 5 V.
questions.figure_alt: Capacitor voltage starting at 2 V and rising toward 5 V.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter with \(\tau=0.25\ \mathrm{ms}\) (capacitor discharged) receives a 5 V step at \(t=0\). What is the slope \(dv_{o}/dt\) of the output immediately after \(t=0\)?
questions.explanation:
From the circuit equation \(v_{o}+\tau\ dv_{o}/dt=v_{s}\): at \(t=0^{+}\), \(v_{o}=0\) and \(v_{s}=5\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(dv_{o}/dt=(v_{s}-v_{o})/\tau=5/0.25\ \mathrm{ms}=20\ \mathrm{V}/\mathrm{ms}\).
Equivalent view: the tangent at \(t=0\) would reach the final value 5 V after exactly one time constant (5 V ÷ 0.25 ms). Common mistake: using the average rate over the first \(\tau\), or \(5\ \mathrm{V}/\mathrm{ms}\).
questions.figure_alt: Step response of an RC filter rising from 0 toward 5 V.

questions.prompt: Preview of open-circuit time constants. A later skill finds a circuit's time constant as \(\tau=R_{\mathrm{th}}\cdot C\), where \(R_{\mathrm{th}}\) is the resistance seen by the capacitor with the independent sources turned off. A node has \(C=2\ \mathrm{nF}\), with 1 kΩ and 4 kΩ resistors connecting it to the source and to ground (the source is an ideal voltage source). After a step, how long does the voltage across C take to reach 90% of its final value?
questions.explanation:
With the source off (a short), the capacitor sees \(1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 4\ \mathrm{k}\Omega=800\ \Omega\).
\(\tau=R_{\mathrm{th}}\cdot C=800\ \Omega\times 2\ \mathrm{nF}=1.6\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). Reaching 90% takes \(t=\tau\ \ln 10=2.303\tau=3.684\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: using \(R_{1}+R_{2}=5\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) (a series sum) instead of the parallel combination.

questions.prompt: Preview of slew rate. An op-amp stage that follows an RC filter \((\tau=2\ \mu\mathrm{s})\) can only change its output by at most \(SR=0.5\ \mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}\). The filter's output has its steepest slope, \(V_{s}/\tau\), right after a step of height \(V_{s}\). What is the largest step \(V_{s}\) that keeps the maximum slope within the slew-rate limit?
questions.explanation:
Maximum slope of the step response: \((dv_{o}/dt)\) at \(t=0^{+}=V_{s}/\tau\). Require \(V_{s}/\tau\le SR\) ⇒ \(V_{s}\le SR\cdot\tau=(0.5\ \mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s})(2\ \mu\mathrm{s})=1\ \mathrm{V}\).
Larger steps force the amplifier into slewing (a straight-line ramp) instead of the clean exponential. Common mistake: using \(\tau\) in the wrong place (\(V_{s}\le SR/\tau\) gives nonsense units).

questions.prompt: Preview of capacitive loading. A common-source amplifier's output node behaves, for small signals, like an RC low-pass with \(R_{o}=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) driving a load capacitance \(C_{L}=50\ \mathrm{pF}\). After a small input step, how long does the output take to settle to within 1% of its final value?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=R_{o}\cdot C_{L}=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\times 50\ \mathrm{pF}=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). Within 1% means \(e^{-t/\tau}=0.01\) ⇒ \(t=\tau\ \ln 100=4.605\tau\).
\(t=4.605\times 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}=2.303\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: using \(1\tau=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (that is the 63% point, not 1% settling).
questions.figure_alt: Normalized step response approaching 1 with a dashed line at 99 percent.
